Injuries are severe, medical bills accumulate quickly, and the trucking company’s insurer often begins preparing its defense before the victim is discharged from the hospital. Trucking cases also tend to involve more parties than a typical car accident: the driver, the trucking company, a cargo loader, or the manufacturer of a defective part may all bear some responsibility, and each may carry separate insurance coverage and separate legal representation.

Types of Truck Accident Cases in Fort Collins, CO

Not all truck accidents unfold the same way, and the type of vehicle involved often plays a large role in how a crash happens and how severe the resulting injuries are. Our team works with clients across a range of commercial vehicle crashes, including the following:
Semi-Trucks and Tractor-Trailers:
These large vehicles are prone to jackknifing, rollovers, and underride collisions, particularly on high-speed corridors such as I-25 and Highway 14.
Delivery and Box Trucks:
Frequent stops and turns in commercial and residential areas increase the risk of collisions with nearby vehicles or pedestrians.
Tow Trucks and Garbage Trucks:
Limited visibility and repeated roadside stops put other drivers at risk, especially in tighter neighborhood streets.
Tanker and Cargo Trucks:
A shifting or spilled load can throw a truck off balance, leading to rollovers or chain-reaction collisions.

The size and weight of these vehicles alone make injuries from a truck crash, on average, more severe than those from a typical passenger vehicle accident. That difference is one reason a thorough investigation into every liable party, from the driver to the trucking company to whoever loaded the cargo, matters so much in these cases.
Common Causes of Truck Accidents in Fort Collins

Truck accidents rarely trace back to a single mistake. Behind most crashes sits a chain of small failures, a missed inspection, a rushed schedule, a driver pushed past the point of safe reaction time, that builds toward something catastrophic.
In Fort Collins and across Larimer County, the most frequent causes include:
Driver Fatigue:
Long hours behind the wheel slow reaction time and impair judgment, especially on overnight freight routes.
Distracted Driving:
Phones, dispatch systems, and in-cab technology divert attention at highway speeds.
Improperly Secured Cargo:
Shifting or falling loads can cause a truck to lose control or trigger a chain-reaction crash.
Poor Vehicle Maintenance:
Worn brakes, bald tires, and neglected inspections turn preventable defects into serious collisions.
Speeding and Aggressive Driving:
Tight delivery schedules push some drivers to take risks that a fully loaded truck cannot safely absorb.
Impaired Driving:
Alcohol, drugs, and even certain prescription medications remain a factor in commercial crashes despite strict federal testing rules.
More than one of these factors is often at play in a single crash, and identifying which ones contributed is part of what a
Fort Collins truck accident lawyer
investigates when determining who can be held responsible.
Injuries Commonly Seen in Truck Accident Cases

Weight and force are what separate a truck crash from an ordinary fender bender, and the resulting injuries reflect it. A loaded semi can weigh twenty times more than the average car, and this weight difference rarely benefits the smaller vehicle.
Victims often face the following injuries:
Traumatic brain injuries, from a sudden impact or jolt causing a concussion or lasting brain damage
Spinal cord injuries, causing chronic pain, partial paralysis, or loss of function below the injury site
Broken bones and fractures, often requiring surgery and months of recovery
Internal organ damage, caused by blunt force trauma not always obvious right after the crash
Severe burns, from fuel leaks or electrical fires, often requiring skin grafts and long-term care
Wrongful death, in the most catastrophic accidents, leaving families grieving on top of financial fallout
Injuries at this level rarely resolve with a simple insurance payout, which is part of what sets a truck accident case apart from an ordinary car accident claim.
Who May Be Liable for a Fort Collins Truck Accident?

Because multiple regulations and multiple companies are often involved, responsibility for a truck accident rarely rests with the driver alone. Depending on what caused the crash, liability may extend to the following parties:
The truck driver, through fatigue, distraction, speeding, or impairment
The trucking company, for pressuring drivers to skip rest, ignoring maintenance, or negligent hiring
A maintenance provider, for failing to properly inspect or repair brakes, tires, or other systems
A cargo loading company, for improperly securing freight, causing a shift or rollover
A parts or vehicle manufacturer, when a defective component contributed to the crash
A government entity, for poor road design, signage, or delayed roadway maintenance
Identifying every liable party takes a thorough investigation, and a
Fort Collins truck accident lawyer
handles it from the moment a case begins.
What Types of Compensation Can You Pursue in a Truck Accident Claim?
Colorado law allows injured victims to pursue full and fair compensation for both current and future losses stemming from the crash. Understanding
what damages in a truck accident case
can include helps set realistic expectations. Depending on the severity of the injuries, a truck accident claim may include the following types of damages:
Medical expenses, covering emergency treatment, surgery, rehabilitation, and ongoing care
Lost wages and earning capacity, covering income missed during recovery and any lasting drop in future earnings
Pain and suffering, for the physical pain and emotional weight that follow a serious crash
Property damage, covering the repair or replacement of a vehicle and other damaged property
Punitive damages, reserved for cases involving fraud, malice, or willful and wanton conduct
The amount a victim can ultimately recover depends heavily on how fault is divided between the parties involved. Colorado follows a modified comparative negligence rule under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-21-111
, reducing a victim’s compensation by the victim’s percentage of fault and barring recovery entirely once that share reaches 50 percent or more.
A filing deadline also applies under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-80-101

, generally allowing three years from the date of a motor vehicle accident to file a civil claim. Certain circumstances may extend or shorten that window, though those situations remain the exception rather than the rule, and determining which deadline applies is best addressed early in the process.
What’s the Average Settlement for a Fort Collins Truck Accident?

There is no set average, since every truck accident case is different. A minor soft tissue injury typically settles for far less than a catastrophic injury requiring surgery or lifelong care. The value of a case is determined by three factors: the seriousness of the injuries, the strength of the evidence of fault, and the amount of insurance coverage available to pay the claim.
Insurance companies often move quickly with an early offer, before an injured party has had a chance to understand the full cost of recovery. At
Dormer Harpring

our attorneys take a different approach, gathering a full picture of the medical needs involved, the income lost, and what recovery may look like months or years later before any settlement discussion begins. That groundwork allows a claim’s value to be evaluated with more complete information before any decision is made.
What To Do After a Truck Accident in Fort Collins, Colorado?
The steps you take immediately after a truck accident can determine the strength of your claim. Knowing
what to do immediately after a truck accident
protects both your health and your case. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 42-4-1601

, every driver involved in a collision must stop, remain at the scene, exchange information, and render reasonable aid to anyone injured. Failing to do so carries criminal penalties separate from any civil claim.
Beyond meeting the legal duty, the following steps can help protect your recovery:
Seek Medical Attention:
Get evaluated even if injuries seem minor, since some symptoms take hours or days to surface.
Document the Scene:
Photograph vehicle positions, cargo, skid marks, and any visible damage before anything is moved.
Preserve Evidence Requests:
Ask your attorney to send preservation letters for driver logs and black box data before the records disappear.
Avoid Recorded Statements:
Insurance adjusters may ask questions designed to minimize your claim before you understand its full value.
Contact a Fort Collins Truck Accident Lawyer:
Early legal guidance protects evidence that disappears quickly after a serious crash.
The earlier these steps are taken, the more difficult it becomes for an insurer to dispute the facts of the case.
What Makes Fort Collins Truck Accident Cases Unique?

A truck accident claim rarely behaves like a typical car accident case, and the difference goes well beyond how severe the injuries tend to be. Federal regulations govern hours of service, cargo securement, and vehicle maintenance, and a violation of any of them can establish negligence, often leading to multiple parties being responsible for the crash.

Location adds another layer to that complexity. Heavy freight traffic moving through the I-25 corridor and along Highway 14 shares the road with local commuters, cyclists, and pedestrians throughout Larimer County, and a crash involving a commercial vehicle in these areas often comes with multiple witnesses, nearby traffic cameras, and overlapping jurisdiction between city and county authorities. A
Fort Collins truck accident lawyer
works through those layers early, since the details tend to matter most before evidence starts to disappear.

faqs.question: Is a police report needed to file a truck accident claim?

children.text: Yes, in most cases. Colorado law requires a police report when a crash causes injury, death, or significant property damage, and that report often becomes an important piece of evidence when building a claim.

faqs.question: Can damages still be recovered if a driver was partly at fault for the crash?

children.text: It depends on the degree of fault. Colorado reduces compensation based on the percentage of fault involved rather than barring a claim outright, as long as that share stays below 50 percent.

faqs.question: Is a trucking company responsible if its driver caused the accident?

children.text: Often, though not always. Trucking companies are typically liable for the negligent actions of their employees while on the job, and their own hiring, training, or maintenance practices can provide an additional basis for liability.
